steps.say: Severe colitis attacks are judged by numbers on day three, not by optimism. When stools stay frequent and the CRP and albumin refuse to improve, rescue treatment starts at once. Infliximab or ciclosporin is given, and the clock keeps ticking. If the colon still shows no improvement by days 4 to 7, the colon comes out before it perforates.
steps.tx: **Acute severe colitis** (fulminant bloody diarrhoea with systemic toxicity) needs rescue **infliximab** (anti-TNF antibody) or **ciclosporin** (calcineurin inhibitor) on day **3** by **Travis criteria** (stool frequency plus CRP and albumin thresholds). Ongoing bleeding and dilatation on days **4 to 7** despite **rescue therapy** (salvage medical treatment) means colectomy, since delay invites perforation.

vis.alt: Illustration comparing Crohn transmural inflammation with ulcerative colitis crypt abscesses.
vis.caption: Ulcerative colitis is mucosal and continuous, unlike transmural Crohn disease. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Young fit patients are offered the pouch operation, which removes the whole colon and rectum yet avoids a permanent bag. The standard build is a J shaped reservoir joined to the anus. Nobody builds a pouch in an emergency or on high dose steroids, the first operation is simply removal of the colon with an ileostomy, and the pouch follows months later.
steps.tx: **Restorative proctocolectomy** (colon and rectum removed with bowel control rebuilt) with **J-pouch** **ileal pouch-anal anastomosis** (small-bowel reservoir joined to the anus) is the choice for fit young patients. Unstable emergency cases and steroid-loaded colons are handled in stages, opening with subtotal colectomy and ileostomy while pouch building waits for fitness months later.

vis.alt: Operative photograph of a matured loop ileostomy in the right iliac fossa on a stoma rod.
vis.caption: Staged surgery starts with subtotal colectomy and ileostomy before pouch building. Credit: Salicyna.

steps.say: Pouch inflammation announces itself with urgency, bleeding and fever in a patient who previously did well. The first treatment is a two week course of ciprofloxacin with metronidazole, which settles most attacks. When the pouch flares every time antibiotics stop, probiotics or biologics are added. Repeated failure points to a mechanical problem that needs surgical revision.
steps.tx: **Pouchitis** (inflammation of the ileal reservoir) with urgency, bleeding and fever responds to **2** weeks of **ciprofloxacin** (quinolone antibiotic) with **metronidazole** (anaerobic antibiotic). Chronic antibiotic-dependent cases step up to probiotics or biologics, and mechanical failure with fistula or stricture needs pouch revision or excision.

steps.say: Long standing extensive colitis grows cancers in flat lining that scopes struggle to see. Once disease has lasted 8 years, any flat dysplasia or stricture means the whole colon and rectum must come out, because a second hidden cancer is likely. Surveillance has already failed that colon, so continued watching only delays the inevitable.
steps.tx: **Flat dysplasia** (invisible abnormal cells in non-raised mucosa) or strictures in longstanding **pancolitis** (whole-colon disease) over **8** years mandates proctocolectomy, because surveillance misses synchronous cancer. Random and targeted biopsies with chromoendoscopy precede the decision, and low-grade change in flat mucosa is not watched.

steps.say: Not every patient needs the full pouch operation. Joining the small bowel straight to the rectal stump avoids pelvic dissection entirely, which protects fertility and nerves in young women and the elderly. The price is a rectal remnant that can still turn malignant, so scopes continue for life. Weak sphincters are also helped by this simpler join.
steps.tx: **Ileorectal anastomosis** (joining ileum to the rectal stump) preserves **fertility preservation** (avoiding pelvic dissection that harms nerves and tubes) and suits older or poor-sphincter patients. The retained rectum keeps cancer risk needing **lifelong surveillance** (annual scopes with biopsies), and uncontrolled rectal inflammation defeats the operation.

points: Rectal stump kept, cancer risk stays
right.title: Price of keeping rectum

steps.say: When pouches fail and the sphincter is gone, the continent ileostomy is the fallback. A Kock pouch with a one way nipple valve holds stool inside without any external bag. It is emptied with a catheter four to six times a day. The weak point is the valve, which can slip and leak, and that needs a repair operation.
steps.tx: Continent **ileostomy** (bag-free **Kock pouch** with a folded ileal reservoir and nipple valve) suits failed pouches and poor sphincters who refuse a conventional **Brooke ileostomy** (end ileostomy with an external bag). The valve needs intubation **4 to 6** times daily, and valve slippage with leakage is the commonest mechanical failure needing revision.

steps.say: Colitis plus sclerosing cholangitis is a dangerous pairing that multiplies cancer risk on two fronts. These patients grow colorectal cancers earlier and can develop bile duct cancer too. Scopes start at diagnosis rather than after years of disease, and dye spray chromoendoscopy is used to catch flat lesions. Liver tests and imaging run alongside.
steps.tx: **Primary sclerosing cholangitis** (scarred beaded bile ducts) alongside ulcerative colitis lifts both colorectal and bile-duct cancer risk, so yearly colonoscopy with **chromoendoscopy** (dye-sprayed mucosal inspection) starts at diagnosis. Tight dominant strictures need brush cytology, and failing livers join the transplant track.

nodes.label: Brush cytology, resect or transplant track

steps.say: Keyhole surgery has earned its place in colitis, giving the same cancer clearance with smaller wounds and faster discharge. But toxic megacolon is the exception that proves the rule. A caecum stretched beyond 9 cm is close to bursting, so these patients go straight to open subtotal colectomy without waiting for laparoscopy or further medicines.
steps.tx: **Laparoscopic colectomy** (keyhole colon removal) equals open resection for cancer clearance while speeding discharge, yet toxic megacolon with a **caecal diameter** (width of the first colon segment) past **9** cm demands urgent open subtotal colectomy. Worsening on medicines with climbing CRP and transfusion need also forces the decision.
